practiceSet.title: U7.LT4 Practice: Mutations
practiceSet.description: Practice what mutations are and what causes them, substitutions (silent, missense, nonsense), frameshifts from insertions and deletions, chromosomal mutations, mutagens, and predicting a mutation's effect on the protein.

activity.title: U7.LT4 Relearning: Mutations
activity.content:
**What you need to be able to do:** I can predict the effects of mutations on DNA.

**Think of a set of LEGO instructions.** Your DNA is a blueprint for your body. A **point mutation** is like a one-letter spelling mistake in the instructions: sometimes it changes nothing, sometimes it changes one step. A **frameshift** is like adding or removing a block from the instructions: every step after it is read wrong. Try it with a sentence of three-letter words: THE CAT ATE THE RAT. Swap one letter (THE CAT ATE THE HAT) and one word changes. Delete one letter (THE CTA TET HER AT) and everything after it is nonsense.

**What a mutation is.** A **mutation** is a change in the DNA sequence. A **gene** is a section of DNA that codes for a protein, so changing a gene can change its protein. (A mistake in one mRNA copy is not a mutation; the DNA is unchanged.)

**Causes.** (1) **Errors during DNA replication**: a wrong base, an extra base, or a missing base. DNA polymerase **proofreading** fixes most of them. (2) **Mistakes during meiosis**: when chromosomes trade pieces to make new combinations, a piece can be lost, copied twice, flipped, or attached to the wrong chromosome. (Normal crossing over, where matching pieces are traded evenly, is not a mutation.) (3) **Environmental factors (mutagens)**: radiation (**UV light, X-rays**), chemicals (**cigarette smoke, nitrite preservatives**), and infectious agents (**HPV**).

**Point mutations: substitutions.** One base is swapped for another. Compare the codons on the chart: **silent** = same amino acid, **missense** = a different amino acid, **nonsense** = the codon becomes a stop codon and the protein is cut short. Sickle cell anemia is a substitution (missense) in the hemoglobin gene.

**Frameshift mutations: insertions and deletions.** Adding (**insertion**) or removing (**deletion**) a base shifts how every later base is grouped into codons, so most amino acids after it change. Adding or removing exactly **3 bases** (one codon) does **not** shift the frame; it adds or removes one amino acid. (The most common cystic fibrosis mutation removes one codon from the CFTR gene.)

**Chromosomal mutations.** Big pieces of chromosomes change, affecting many genes at once: **deletion** (a piece is lost), **duplication** (a piece is copied an extra time), **inversion** (a piece flips around, as in some forms of hemophilia), and **translocation** (a piece moves to a different chromosome).

**Effects.** Mutations can be **harmful, neutral, or beneficial** (beneficial ones help species evolve). Mutations in genes that control the cell cycle can lead to **cancer**. Only mutations in **sperm or egg cells** are passed to children; mutations in body cells stay in that person, though they are copied into the new cells when that cell divides.

**How to predict an effect:** write the original mRNA and the mutated mRNA, group both into codons from the start codon, translate both with the chart, and compare.

**Worked example 1:** Chart: AUG = Met, UCA = Ser, AAA = Lys, UAA = Stop. The mRNA AUG-UCA-AAA codes for Met-Ser-Lys. A substitution changes AAA to UAA. Step 1: Look up the new codon: UAA = stop. Step 2: The protein ends right there. **Answer:** a nonsense mutation; the protein is only Met-Ser.

**Worked example 2:** Chart: AUG = Met, CCG = Pro, UAU = Tyr, GGA = Gly, CGU = Arg. The mRNA AUG-CCG-UAU-GGA codes for Met-Pro-Tyr-Gly. The first C of CCG is deleted. Step 1: New mRNA: AUGCGUAUGGA. Step 2: Regroup from the start: AUG-CGU-AUG-GA. Step 3: Translate: Met-Arg-Met. **Answer:** a frameshift; every amino acid after Met changed.

**Worked example 3:** A chromosome's genes are A-B-C-D-E-F. After a mutation they read A-B-C-D-E-D-E-F. Step 1: No genes are missing or flipped, and none came from another chromosome. Step 2: D-E appears twice. **Answer:** a duplication.

**Watch out for:** looking up DNA triplets on the mRNA codon chart (transcribe first); thinking every mutation is harmful; thinking a substitution always changes the protein (it can be silent); thinking a 3-base insertion or deletion shifts the frame; thinking body-cell mutations are inherited; and calling an mRNA copying mistake a mutation.
prompts: The mRNA AUG-UAC-GGA codes for Met-Tyr-Gly. Chart: UAU = Tyr, UAA = Stop, GCA = Ala. Classify each change as silent, missense, or nonsense, and explain: (a) UAC → UAU, (b) UAC → UAA, (c) GGA → GCA.
Use the sentence THE FAT CAT SAW THE DOG to show a substitution, an insertion, and a deletion. Explain which kind of change messes up the most words, and why.
List the three main causes of mutations and give one example of each.
Explain why a mutation in a skin cell caused by a sunburn can't be passed on to a person's children, but a mutation in an egg cell can.
